questions.stem: What BEST distinguishes using a drive wipe tool from overwriting a drive by hand?

options.rationale: Correct: the tool erases the whole drive and documents it.
Both approaches allow reuse.
Wiping leaves the drive usable.
A proper wipe makes data unrecoverable.

questions.explanation: A drive wipe is a tool-driven erase of the whole drive (wipe utilities, firmware secure erase, cryptographic erase), often with verification. It is automated and reportable, supports reuse, and typically applies overwrite.
questions.discriminator_tested: Drive wipe: automated and reportable.

questions.stem: Which two are physical destruction methods for drives? (Choose two.)

options.rationale: Correct.
Correct: it destroys magnetic media (not SSDs).
An overwrite leaves the drive reusable.
A wipe method; the drive survives.
Leaves data recoverable.

questions.explanation: Physical destruction means shredding, crushing, incineration, or degaussing (magnetic media). It is the most certain method and leaves the drive unusable; degaussing doesn't work on SSDs.
questions.discriminator_tested: Destruction is most certain; degaussing doesn't work on SSDs.

questions.stem: Ransomware encrypted a file server and also the backup share mapped on that server, and restores now fail. What was the MAIN weakness?

options.text: No offline or offsite backup copy
options.rationale: Correct: the ransomware could reach every copy.
A real gap, but even tested backups were reachable here.
Might explain the infection, not the failed recovery.
Size isn't why they failed.

questions.explanation: Data backups are copies of data for recovery after loss, failure, or ransomware. An untested backup is unproven, and offline or offsite copies resist ransomware.
questions.discriminator_tested: Offline or offsite copies resist ransomware.

questions.stem: What BEST distinguishes regulatory compliance from internal security policy?

options.text: Compliance requirements are imposed from outside
options.rationale: Correct: laws and industry rules such as HIPAA and PCI DSS.
True, but internal policies are audited too.

options.text: Policy is enforced by law; compliance is optional
options.rationale: This is reversed.

options.text: They are the same thing with different names
options.rationale: One is external, the other internal.

questions.explanation: Regulatory compliance means meeting external legal and industry requirements for handling data (for example HIPAA, PCI DSS, GDPR). It is externally imposed, unlike internal policy.
questions.discriminator_tested: Compliance is externally imposed.

questions.stem: A company wants to fully wipe any lost phone remotely, with no staff privacy concerns. Which device model BEST fits?

options.rationale: Correct: full organizational control, no personal data at stake.
Possible, but wiping personal phones raises privacy issues.

options.text: BYOD phones with a screen-lock rule
options.rationale: A screen lock doesn't allow remote wiping.
No control at all.

questions.explanation: BYOD means employee-owned devices; organization-owned devices are under full organizational control. Ownership drives how much control and privacy there is.
questions.discriminator_tested: Ownership drives control and privacy.

questions.stem: A company needs to enroll 500 phones, push Wi-Fi and email settings to them, and remotely lock lost ones. What BEST fits?

options.rationale: Correct: enroll, configure, and enforce policy centrally.

options.text: An asset tag on each phone
options.rationale: Tags identify devices; they don't manage them.
A portal gates network access; it doesn't manage phones.
A SIEM analyzes logs.

questions.explanation: MDM is a central platform to enroll, configure, and enforce policy on mobile devices, including remote lock and wipe. Configuration management, app distribution, and encryption are things it manages.
questions.discriminator_tested: MDM is the platform.

questions.stem: A management tool produces the report below. What BEST describes what it shows?
questions.exhibit:
Baseline: WIN11-STD v4 (approved 2026-09-01)
Host      Setting                     Baseline   Actual
LT-0112   SMBv1                       Disabled   Enabled
LT-0112   Firewall (Public profile)   On         Off
LT-0157   (no deviations)

options.rationale: Correct: LT-0112 no longer matches the approved configuration.
True, but it doesn't name what the report detects.
Nothing here is about patches.
LT-0157 has no deviations at all.

questions.explanation: Configuration management maintains consistent, documented, approved configurations (baselines) under change control, which lets it detect configuration drift.
questions.discriminator_tested: Baseline plus change control detects drift.

questions.stem: Managed phones may install apps from a company-approved catalog and nowhere else. Which MDM capability does this describe?

options.rationale: Correct: governs software sources on managed devices.
Protects stored data, not app sources.
Settings consistency, not app sources.
Erases a lost device.

questions.explanation: App distribution controls which apps are installed and from where (a managed app store, allow and block lists). It governs software sources on managed devices.
questions.discriminator_tested: App distribution governs software sources.

questions.stem: A managed laptop has full-disk encryption. Which risk does this MOST directly reduce?

options.text: Data exposure if the device is lost
options.rationale: Correct: the disk is unreadable without the key.

options.text: Malware infection while it is in use
options.rationale: While running, the disk is unlocked.
Email filtering and training address that.
Disk encryption doesn't touch network traffic.

questions.explanation: Data encryption protects data on the device, for example with full-disk encryption. A lost or stolen device doesn't expose readable data.
questions.discriminator_tested: Lost or stolen device doesn't expose readable data.

questions.stem: What BEST distinguishes endpoint recovery from endpoint protection?

options.rationale: Correct: after a problem vs before it.
True of recovery, but it doesn't contrast it with protection.
Continuous scanning is protection.

options.text: They are two names for EDR
options.rationale: EDR is one protection control.

questions.explanation: Endpoint recovery restores an endpoint to a known-good state (restore from backup, reimage, rebuild) after a problem; endpoint protection tries to prevent the problem.
questions.discriminator_tested: Recovery after a problem; protection tries to prevent it.

questions.stem: Which two are endpoint protection controls? (Choose two.)

options.rationale: Correct: detective and responsive control on the device.
Correct: preventive control on the device.
Supports recovery, not protection.

options.text: An IP scanner on the subnet
options.rationale: A network discovery tool.
A disposal tool.

questions.explanation: Endpoint protection is the controls on the device itself: antimalware, host-based firewall, host intrusion detection, and EDR. They are preventive and detective controls on the endpoint.
questions.discriminator_tested: Preventive and detective controls on the endpoint itself.

questions.stem: What is the MAIN trade-off of cloud-based endpoint protection?

options.text: Fast updates, but it needs internet
options.rationale: Correct: fast and works off-network, but relies on connectivity.
The benefit, without the trade-off.

options.text: It replaces the need for local agents
options.rationale: It still relies on an agent on each endpoint.

options.text: It works on the office network alone
options.rationale: It covers devices off-network too.

questions.explanation: Cloud-based protection delivers or analyzes endpoint security through the cloud (cloud signatures, threat intelligence, a central console). It gives fast updates and off-network coverage but needs connectivity.
questions.discriminator_tested: Fast updates and off-network coverage; needs connectivity.

questions.stem: An analyst reviews the scan history below for one laptop. What do these logs MOST importantly show?
questions.exhibit:
Scheduled scan  LT-0201  2026-10-14 02:00  Completed  0 threats  Defs: 2026-07-30
Scheduled scan  LT-0201  2026-10-15 02:00  Failed     service stopped
Scheduled scan  LT-0201  2026-10-16 02:00  Failed     service stopped

options.rationale: Correct: scans aren't running, and definitions are months old.

options.text: No threats were found on 14 October
options.rationale: True, but meaningless with outdated definitions.

options.text: The laptop is free of malware
options.rationale: A clean log doesn't prove safety.
They are failing, not too frequent.

questions.explanation: Reviewing scan logs means examining antimalware and vulnerability scan results for detections, failures, and patterns. A clean log doesn't prove safety; check that scans ran and definitions were current.
questions.discriminator_tested: A clean log doesn't prove safety.

questions.stem: Which sequence matches the malware remediation process?

options.text: Identify, quarantine, disable Restore, remediate, update, enable Restore, educate
options.rationale: Correct: the seven steps in order.

options.text: Quarantine, identify, remediate, disable Restore, update, enable Restore, educate
options.rationale: Symptoms are confirmed first, and Restore is disabled before cleaning.

options.text: Identify, quarantine, remediate, disable Restore, enable Restore, update, educate
options.rationale: Restore must be off before cleaning, and updates come before re-enabling it.

options.text: Identify, remediate, quarantine, educate, disable Restore, update, enable Restore
options.rationale: Quarantine must come before cleaning.

questions.explanation: The malware remediation process has seven ordered steps: identify and verify symptoms; quarantine; disable System Restore; remediate; schedule scans and run updates; re-enable System Restore and create restore points; educate users.
questions.discriminator_tested: Sequence matters.

questions.stem: A user reports pop-ups, a changed browser home page, and antivirus that won't start. Following the malware remediation process, what is the FIRST step?

options.rationale: Correct: confirm the symptoms before acting.

options.text: Disconnect the PC from the network
options.rationale: Quarantine is the second step.
Scanning is part of remediation, step four.
Premature, and not the first step.

questions.explanation: Identifying and verifying malware symptoms means gathering the signs (slowness, pop-ups, redirects, disabled antivirus, unknown processes) and confirming malware. It is the first step: confirm before acting.
questions.discriminator_tested: First step: confirm before acting.

questions.stem: A PC is confirmed infected with a worm. Per the malware remediation process, what should the technician do NEXT?

options.rationale: Correct: quarantine stops the spread before cleaning.
Cleaning comes after quarantine and disabling Restore.
That is the step after quarantine.
Education is the last step.

questions.explanation: Quarantining an infected system means isolating it from the network (disconnecting it or moving it to an isolated VLAN). It stops the spread before cleaning.
questions.discriminator_tested: Quarantine stops spread before cleaning.

questions.stem: What BEST explains why System Restore is turned off before cleaning an infected Windows PC?

options.text: Restore points may hold copies of the malware
options.rationale: Correct: they could reintroduce it later.

options.text: It is a required step in the process
options.rationale: True, but it doesn't say why.

options.text: It frees disk space for the scan
options.rationale: Space isn't the reason.

options.text: It stops the malware spreading on the network
options.rationale: Quarantine does that.

questions.explanation: Disabling System Restore before cleaning keeps malware in old restore points from being preserved, because restore points can hold malware.
questions.discriminator_tested: Restore points can hold malware.

questions.stem: A rootkit hides from the antivirus while Windows is running. Which approach BEST removes it?

options.rationale: Correct: the rootkit can't hide when its OS isn't running.
Necessary, but the rootkit still hides from a scan run inside Windows.
UAC has nothing to do with detection.
That destroys Windows.

questions.explanation: Remediating infected systems means updating antimalware, scanning, and removing the malware, using safe mode or rescue media when needed. Use current definitions; rescue media helps with stealthy malware such as rootkits.
questions.discriminator_tested: Rescue media helps with stealthy malware such as rootkits.

questions.stem: Malware got in through an unpatched browser plug-in and has now been removed. What BEST explains why the process still requires patching and scheduled scans?

options.text: To close the hole that let it in
options.rationale: Correct: otherwise the same flaw lets it straight back in.

options.text: To keep the antivirus definitions current
options.rationale: Part of it, but patching the entry point matters most.

options.text: To restore the files the malware deleted
options.rationale: Patches don't restore files.
That is the next step, not this one's purpose.

questions.explanation: Scheduling scans and running updates means patching the OS and applications, updating signatures, and scheduling recurring scans. It closes the hole that let the malware in.
questions.discriminator_tested: Closes the hole that let the malware in.

questions.stem: When should System Restore be turned back on and a new restore point created?

options.text: After the system is verified clean
options.rationale: Correct: so the restore point captures a clean state.
The PC is still infected then.
A restore point then would capture the malware.

options.text: It stays off on a previously infected PC
options.rationale: It should be re-enabled once the PC is clean.

questions.explanation: Turn System Restore back on and create a fresh restore point only after the system is verified clean.
questions.discriminator_tested: Only after the system is verified clean.

questions.stem: A user's PC was cleaned of malware that arrived in a phishing email. A week later it is reinfected the same way. Which step was MOST likely skipped?

options.rationale: Correct: the final step prevents a repeat.
Scans can't stop a user clicking a link.
That affects cleanup, not how the user got phished again.
Quarantine contains spread during cleaning.

questions.explanation: Educating end users (phishing, safe downloads, reporting) is the final step of the malware remediation process, and it prevents recurrence.
questions.discriminator_tested: Education is the final step; prevents recurrence.
